utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Bosanac, if I could remind you of the affirmation you made at the commencement of your evidence, which still applies. I would also mention that word has been passed to me from the Victims and Witnesses Unit that Dr. Bosanac is concerned whether she might look at the transcript of the proceedings on Friday, as she has a concern that she confused some documents in giving her evidence. I thought I would mention that in court before acting on it, to see whether there was any concern at that occurring. If there is no concern, we will arrange for that to occur. It probably won't be convenient for that to occur before you finish your evidence today, Doctor. If you look at the evidence overnight and feel you have a concern that you made a mistake, that word can be passed to the Chamber and we will arrange for you to be recalled tomorrow to clarify whatever it is that concerns you. Is that satisfactory? Very well. Thank you for that. Now, Mr. Lukic, were you in the course of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to my friends and colleagues from the OTP. Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the witness. I will now continue with my cross-examination of the witness. As for the following set of questions that I'm about to ask you, could you please focus exclusively on the number of wounded and sick who were in fact in the hospital as patients in the last days before the war -- before the fall. Can you please exclude medical staff, the families of the medical staff wounded from this reckoning. You told me on Friday, during your testimony on examination-in-chief, that on the 18th of November, there were no new sick or wounded persons registered at the hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the last wounded and ill persons to be registered in the hospital were registered on the 17th or on the 18th? Can you perhaps remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that from the 18th of November on, not one new wounded person was admitted into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that you forwarded this information to Zagreb, more specifically to Dr. Hebrang, in relation to your negotiations on evacuation.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We spoke on the phone and I told him at the time that there were about 400 wounded and sick to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, let's take one thing at a time. I'm just asking you about whether you forwarded that specific bit of information to Hebrang or not. Perhaps for the benefit of the Chamber, let us be more specific about this. Who was Mr. Hebrang at the time? Which position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the health Minister of the Republic of Croatia. He negotiated on the evacuation on behalf of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please try to think back? What I want to know is do you remember, concerning the number of the wounded and ill in the hospital on that day, or on those days, the 17th, the 18th or perhaps the 20th, the last days before the fall, how many were envisaged to be transported out of the hospital in an ambulance, having been classified as immobile, and how many of them were actually able to get on to buses and be taken away on buses? Is this something you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that at the time, there were about 400 wounded and ill persons in the hospital. About half of them, between 180 and 200 required transport by an ambulance. Those people were either seriously wounded or immobile, were not able to walk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all of the wounded and sick persons wish to be taken back to Croatia during the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We drew up lists and we took this into account. Most of those requested to go back to Croatia. Some requested to go to Belgrade or Novi Sad and some of them in fact requested to remain where they were in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that about 110 wounded and sick requested to go to Belgrade and Novi Sad? Is this something that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that some of them did in fact request that but I do not remember their specific number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the claim, Novi Sad, where is Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novi Sad is in Vojvodina, Yugoslavia, now Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to Mr. Hebrang on the phone about the specific numbers of persons and the facilities to be used during the evacuation, ambulances, and so on and so forth, did he mention that there might be trouble, that he might be facing a lot of trouble organising the requested number of ambulances and other technical necessities?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never said he believed they would be facing any difficulty with that. He only said that the first stretch of the evacuation route would be secured by the International Red Cross and the Yugoslav army jointly. And the stretch from Nustar on would have ambulances and medical vehicles waiting for the wounded to be taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, on the 17th, when you spoke to Hebrang you told him that there were between 180 and 200 wounded that required transport by special medical vehicles, isn't that what you told him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correction, line -- it's been corrected. Thank you. You testified on Thursday, the 27th, about there being about 180 seriously wounded persons and a total of 400 people to be included in the evacuation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two days earlier, before this very same Trial Chamber, you spoke about 450 people needing evacuation. You said that on the 25th, page 15 of the transcript. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about these same figures in your statement to the investigators of the OTP in 1995. On the occasion you said that on the 17th of November, you had a total of 250 wounded persons and over 100 elderly and sick. You did say that in 1995. I suppose you've gone through your statement since. You saw it the other day; it was shown to you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I did read it again. However this is a statement that I gave back in 1995 and I can no longer remember with any degree of accuracy what exactly I said. I know there were between 400 and 450 wounded and sick persons at the hospital but I can't be very specific about the figures right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it's been only two days and the discrepancy amounts to 50 persons. So that seems like a significant figure to me.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certainly not all right, but there is something I wish to clarify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the last days all of those who arrived, I'm talking about the lightly wounded with surface wounds, dislocated joints, the hospital was brimful with these people. We would dress their wounds and just send them off to nearby shelters. As I said before, in early November, the route along Priljevo street had been blocked. This is a road that we used to transport the wounded to Borovo Komerc, which had a shelter. After that we took them to the Olajnica neighbourhood local shelter and to the Ivolola Riber [phoen] school building shelter. There were plenty of those who could have been classified as slightly wounded. They were not registered as patients of our hospital but I envisaged them to be part of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were not in the hospital itself in those days as in-patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when negotiations took place in Zagreb between Mr. Hebrang and General Raseta? Is this something that Mr. Hebrang shared with you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. We spoke on the phone almost on a daily basis and he said that there were continuing negotiations throughout that week, virtually on a daily basis. There had been negotiations to do with previous attempts and previous evacuations. They were having negotiations about this last evacuation throughout that week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When do you think this round of negotiations drew to a close?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe on the 17th. It was a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the Registrar could please show the witness the following document: MFI 40, ID. The so-called Zagreb agreement. If we could please have that displayed on the screen? [In English] Marked for identification, 40. [Interpretation] Can you see it? This is an English copy of the document. Do you think we could have a B/C/S version displayed, Mr. Usher, if I can have your assistance, please? [In English] The B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must be a printed copy, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll provide one so you don't have to worry about that. Can you please look at paragraph 1 of the document and tell us what you see. When did these negotiations take place and when was the agreement allegedly signed? That's in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that. It says they met on the 18th of November and reached an agreement and so on and so forth, "the following agreement," it says. However this is not something that I can comment on, given the fact that I wasn't present at this meeting. I know that on the 17th, the previous Sunday, I had been informed about an evacuation that was to take place on the 18th in the morning hours. Now, as to when exactly the agreement was signed, at what time and how, is something I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph 4 of the agreement? You provided information to Mr. Hebrang. This is something you told me a minute ago. How come we see the following figures, 40 seriously ill and 360 casualties?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I gave the exact information that I gave to you a while ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, 360 or so casualties of whom around a third will require stretchers. There was a typo or some sort of misunderstanding that occurred. That much is obvious.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, is there a single word in this document in front of you referring to civilians? Do you see a single reference to civilian persons or medical staff in this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read the entire document or what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know had been agree. I'm telling you about the information that I provided on that occasion. If you want me to go through the document, I can. I can read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no need for you to do that. I'm just putting it to you that you said, in your examination-in-chief, that Mr. Hebrang had told you that the wounded and ill would be the first to be evacuated and that the civilians would not be evacuated until the next day but you did not in fact see the specific agreement in which there is no reference whatsoever to anything like this. Let's move on. We shall no longer be requiring this document, thank you. Can we now please go back to the appeals that you wrote? Can the witness please be shown the following document, the Exhibit 22? We had a problem identifying this document because it had first been marked as 21. The date on the appeal, on the call for help, is the 3rd of November. That's right. Do you see the document on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went through this document on examination-in-chief, and you told us that all the information provided in these appeals were accurate and based on information you had obtained from your own unit, your own service.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we please just try to track down a printed copy? Because the -- this is very difficult for me to read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Should be fine now. Can you follow now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly did you ascertain on that day about the number of wounded and ill in your hospital? What does it say here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 350.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can the witness now please be shown Exhibit 23? Would you please zoom in? Could it be enlarged? Can you see how many patients you had on the following day in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that, 270.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please explain how come you released 70 or 80 patients in one day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, we released whomever we could and released them to the local shelters. In the Borovo Komerc shelter we had an auxiliary hospital running and also there were over 15 other shelters throughout Vukovar and Borovo Naselje where we also sent those who were ready to be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown Exhibit 34, please? [In English] Exhibit 34. [Interpretation] This is your telephone message, as you have described to us, dated on the 18th of November at 0850?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many patients did you have then?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 600 patients, plus about 200 in the auxiliary hospital in Borovo Komerc. I expected them to be evacuated at the same time as the people from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you stated that there were 600 patients in the hospital. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I had in mind was 400 patients in the hospital plus 200 in Borovo Komerc which was an auxiliary hospital where there were also patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we now be shown Exhibit 37? Could we please see the enlarged print? This was composed on the same day, at 1540. This is your message. So several hours later, how many wounded did you have?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote down "over 500."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which could be 1.000, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be. But I wrote down here "over 500," because I had in mind those who were in the hospital and those in the vicinity. That's what I had in mind when I gave this figure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps have in mind those who were put on patient lists even though they were not patients? And this is how this number came to be so large, increased so rapidly?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have them in mind. Whom I had in mind were the people in the shelters in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is your claim that you did not manipulate with the figure of the wounded and patients in your calls for help?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not manipulate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro, on the 19th, in the afternoon, was he in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he also gave a statement to the OTP at the same time you did?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that he is one of the persons who was very actively involved in the hospital staff, was quite familiar with what was happening at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also claims that Sljivancanin arrived together with Borsinger at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He might have seen that when he arrived in the evening with Borsinger, and I can tell you that in the afternoon I came out of the hospital and (redacted) Dr. Njavro left the hospital and went outside. They were inside in the basement. Therefore, they were unable to know when he arrived there the first time, I think, because they were in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're claiming that the civilians were taken out in the afternoon hours?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was still light upon my return from Negoslavci, it was around 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's just take it slowly. Who is Zeljka Zgonjanin?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljka Zgonjanin is a lady who worked as a representative of the Croatian Red Cross in Vukovar, the city of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she compile a list of civilians?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Binazija Kolesar was your head nurse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Binazija Kolesar move around the hospital in those days or did she mostly sit in the office?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She moved around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you what she said to The Hague investigators when she gave a statement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: She claims that civilians were taken in the evening when it was dark, that she approached civilians asking them where they were going, and that civilians told her that Zeljka Zgonjanin had organised for them to be transported in the trucks. So this is what your head nurse stated. Did she have any reasons to lie to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think she had any reasons to lie but I believe that she wasn't sufficiently informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Binazija Kolesar even claims that she didn't see a single soldier, JNA soldier or paramilitary soldier, taking any civilians out of the hospital that night. At that point in time, you had already been taken to Negoslavci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Binazija Kolesar was unable to see that because she was in the hospital in the basement, and this was taking place in the courtyard of the hospital. The door which was normally closed was open at the time, and civilians who were in the hospital were being taken out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how, then, was Binazija Kolesar, who was in the basement, able to talk with civilians who were in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where she talked with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I object to the line of questioning because my learned friend Mr. Lukic is asking the witness to give opinion evidence by way of explanation of what Kolesar saw or did not see. It's a -- the correct approach in my submission is to ask questions in relation to what this witness saw, ask Kolesar what she saw, if there is a disparity to draw the Court's attention to it in due course, but how can this witness pass or give evidence on something that she herself says that she does not know and did not see? She is being asked to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, though, Mr. Moore, it is fair that the witness have an opportunity to comment on any different account of the facts by somebody such as the witness Kolesar, or the potential witness Kolesar, in case there is some explanation that readily occurs to Dr. Bosanac. So that in that respect, I disagree with your submission. But it is also correct, Mr. Lukic, that you are going further than that and you are trying to get this witness to give an explanation for differences and she simply may not be in that position. And if that's the case, that's all she can say. She understands one set of facts. If somebody else understands another, she cannot comment further. But I think it's proper for you to draw to her attention the significant differences as you see them and see whether she does have any explanation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I put the question based on the opinion of this witness that Binazija Kolesar was unable to see these things, so this is what she stated herself based on which I put this additional question as to -- the witness was able to see that. However, I do accept your suggestions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any rate, Mrs. Bosanac, you're aware of the fact that Binazija Kolesar in the afternoon and in the evening, as head nurse, was in the hospital building and was moving about the building. You are aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after all of these things that I put to you, all of these claims, you still stand by your statement that the civilians were taken in the afternoon, that Sljivancanin came in the afternoon, and Borsinger only came in the evening?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm stating that because that was my experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood it that you were shocked by the fact that civilians were taken in the afternoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why is it that you never mentioned that to Mr. Borsinger when you talked to them in the evening?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why I didn't state that? I told him that we had been waiting for two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I heard you say that. But please don't repeat that. What I'm asking you is: Why did you not ask him about this fact that shocked you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, at that point in time I was focused on the evacuation of the hospital and I believed that to be a priority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Mr. Sljivancanin, when he was in the hospital, he toured the room, visited the room, where the Crisis Staff was in the hospital? He wanted to see that room. Did he say anything about that, and can you tell us how far that building is from the main hospital building?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of the hospital does not exist as a separate room. The Crisis Staff of the hospital held meetings in August in the old administration building which was totally destroyed. At that point in time, everything took place in the basement of the hospital in the room where I was, which could fit only three to four people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there isn't a building in the vicinity of the main hospital building which housed the staff?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me this: Several days ago, when you testified in your examination-in-chief, you said that only a part of the medical documentation pertaining to the wounded was ready for evacuation and that a large portion remained there and that it is now missing, as though the hospital never operated in 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, whose documentation were you able to prepare? Documentation of which patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We prepared for evacuation all patients who were wounded and who were in the hospital, and their documentation. However, that documentation was not evacuated with us. Rather, it remained in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that each patient had a bag with his or her documentation on him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, then, did you say several days ago that you'd only prepared documents for a limited number of patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said for those who had been wounded previously. I said we had the documents in their entirety in two boxes for x-rays to be taken away belonging to those hospitals who were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did each and every patient about to be evacuated have their medical files, their case histories on them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that for us, doctor. You testified today, and I believe my colleague Mr. Vasic asked you the same question, that you were sending information on the numbers of patients to Zagreb on virtually a daily basis. You said that on Friday, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were those reports made up of? What sort of information did they include? Did they have first and last names, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and last names, addresses, diagnosis, ethnic background, and status as a police officer, civilian, soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When exactly did you begin to send those reports?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified on Friday that when you reached Zagreb and were eventually free, you had occasion to look at some of those reports that you had previously written. Did you in fact and where was that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dating to which period?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: August, September, October, all the way until the 6th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to send reports after the 6th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We typed them into the computer and we sent printed copies too, but I never actually saw those arrive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask Mr. Hebrang or whoever was in charge of those documents why the other reports from after the 6th of November were missing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that there had been a communication breakdown, the lines broke down after that date and the reports were no longer able to reach them via computer, and the same applied to the printed copies. Those that were meant for the defence staff, for the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and for the Red Cross. All those remained in the hospital. I was never aware of anyone taking those files away. I think they all stayed back at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were printed copies forwarded, by fax?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by fax.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is not a single printed copy at the health ministry dated after the 6th of November, but the appeals are there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The appeals are there because those documents were preserved by some ladies working for the European Commission Monitoring Mission and they later gave me these reports when I was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the printed copies that were sent after the 6th of November? Those were destroyed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what I know about the fate of those documents. And at this point, I am no longer to tell you anything else. Maybe there should be a court order sent to one of these institutions. The defence ministry, Ministry of Internal Affairs or the Croatian Red Cross, to have a look and see if they can track down any of those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact ever request from the International Red Cross the specific lists that you gave to Borsinger on the 18th? Did you ever request that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We requested many things over the years, but the only thing that we were able to obtain was the list of people who were eventually evacuated on those two days. 120 on the 20th of November and another 54 wounded on the next day, a total of 174 wounded. We have lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know all these things.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know whether you know about these things? We haven't spoken about these things so far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe the Prosecutor might be asking these questions on re-examination because this needs clarifying but what I want to know for the time being is whether, on the 17th or the 18th, you sent any printed reports to Zagreb about the numbers of wounded, sick, and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that on those days, those three days I was no longer able to fax or phone any messages. I just used the phone link to give them the total of wounded persons at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I put it to you that those reports containing the names of the wounded and ill, even if they in fact existed, would not be convenient for your authorities because they would show the exact numbers of those wounded and ill who ended up in Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not right in saying that because I have 97 wounded people who were registered at Ovcara and I have the list on me in case you're interested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You identified those persons as wounded based on the bandages they wore or what?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Based on our database, the database that we had in our computer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the Zagreb-based health ministry?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to which I have to state the following. I'm not sure if you're familiar with this. As for the identification of those killed or executed at Ovcara, was conducted by the American -- by an American forensic team and their post-mortems contain all of the conclusions and findings that they reached. There is no doubt about the fact that findings that they reached. There is no doubt about the fact that these people were wounded and ill, the people that we are talking about now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now be asking you a couple of questions about -- just a minute, please. Can you just please tell me: Where was this database on patients that you kept? Was it in the Vukovar Hospital or in Zagreb and where in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean now or back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, it was in our computer in the Vukovar Hospital and it was forwarded to the medical headquarters of the health ministry in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 6th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the computer that you had in the hospital? Where exactly did you keep this database?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was later taken to Belgrade. I saw it in the press later on, in a newspaper called Ilustrovana Politika. One of the JNA soldiers were in fact using that computer. There was a photograph in December 1991 that I remember looking at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the shelter of the Crisis Staff in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such thing as a Crisis Staff shelter. The Crisis Staff was not inside a shelter. The only persons inside the shelter were those seriously wounded, women, and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about your conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin in Negoslavci on the evening of the 19th. How long did that interrogation last, in your estimate, in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About half an hour, up to 40 minutes, I reckon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this person, I'm not sure what his name was. I refer to him as captain in my statement because I heard him called that in Mitrovica. Sasa he was there, Major Sljivancanin, and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The three of you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please try to think back clearly and tell me exactly whether you remember if during your interrogation at Negoslavci a camcorder was on all the time and whether the whole interview was in fact recorded. Is this something you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "No," does that mean you don't remember or you're actually certain that no camcorder was there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'm quite sure I was recorded at the barracks but not in Negoslavci. I don't think there was one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that occasion, you told the then Major Sljivancanin that on the last day a large number of National Guards Corps members arrived in the hospital and that you opposed this, that you opposed them entering the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that a large number of civilians had arrived, and this was something that I had opposed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why oppose civilians being there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the hospital was overcrowded as it was with wounded and ill. We had no running water, no electricity. They came. They were there for two days just squatting around. We had nothing but tea to give children to drink.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was your reason?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about the morning of the 20th, the 20th of November when you were returned to the hospital from Negoslavci. Prior to the meeting at Gipsara, do you remember that you were with Sljivancanin and Dr. Ivezic, another Colonel in your office, the two of them were alone with you at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an officer, carrying a rifle, who was in the room throughout. He was with me throughout. He answered the phone and he wouldn't allow me to answer the phone myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we know that. But what about the morning?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was returned at about 6.30 in the morning and there was one man there with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that this doctor, Colonel, from the military -- the medical academy tell you personally that the patients had to be brought in and examined?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that. I just remember that Sljivancanin told me that I was no longer in charge of the hospital, that I should convene all of my staff in the plaster room, so-called plaster room. That's all I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be wrong in saying that you yourself in fact proposed that this meeting take place, the meeting with the medical staff and the doctors who arrived from the military medical academy to deal with these medical examinations would I be wrong in saying that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin requested that we find the biggest room possible in which we could meet. I told him that the best place to meet was the so-called plaster room because that was the only vacant empty room or hall inside the whole hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about this doctor you said was with him then. You said there were about six or seven persons there, that's what you said isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's what I saw in the plaster room when I came. They were just standing there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether any of them said to set up mixed teams of doctors who would then examine patients? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not something that I heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were six or seven doctors who arrived in the plaster room along with Major Sljivancanin. You did say that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were taken from the plaster room back to your office, I expect, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that you talked with Mr. Sljivancanin alone at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just know that there was that one man there who was watching me and keeping me from answering the phone myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember you actually asked Sljivancanin what would become of you now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether you would be allowed to go back to your family in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believed at the time that the hospital would be evacuated, that I would remain and go to Borovo Komerc in order to help with evacuating the wounded and ill from Komerc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Sljivancanin asking you about an officer named Rajko Tomic and that, in Sljivancanin's presence, you made a phone call to Zagreb to ask about this Rajko Tomic, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I read about this in Sljivancanin's book but it's not something that I remember happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that in your presence he called someone on that same phone asking them what to do with you? You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to hear about some details. I find this very interesting. Can you please describe this interrogation in the barracks basement on the evening of the 20th? Who brought you there, how long were you there for, what did you talk about, and who exactly was there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent the whole day in the barracks with Marin Vidic in a first floor room. The man who brought us there came back at about 6.00 in the afternoon, late in the afternoon. He said the situation had changed, the major was facing some sort of difficulty, the evacuation had been completed, and that we will to stay there and spend the night. He took us to a different room with many beds in it, and we just sat down, each of us on one bed and we were being guarded throughout, watched throughout. At about 10.00 in the evening a soldier came into the room and told me to follow him. Marin also stood up to follow but he told him to stay put and took me downstairs. I think it was the ground floor that he took me to but I'm not certain. There were several officers waiting there, wearing camouflage uniforms. There was one lady, also wearing a camouflage uniform. They had cameras there, camcorders, and they asked me whether I agreed to give a statement. I asked what sort of statement? They said well, about the situation at the hospital. I said I had nothing against that. And eventually I gave some sort of a statement there, I'm not sure how long it took. It may have taken about 15 minutes, between 10 and 15 minutes. The lady spoke to me in such a way that I felt a certain amount of hostility. They all appeared to be angry with me. Her son had been a soldier. He was in the barracks. And the barracks came under fire. I remember the details of that conversation. I was then taken outside the barracks in a Black Maria paddy wagon, the sort of vehicle they use to transport prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We heard about this already. Can we now please go through the statement that the witness gave at the Sremska Mitrovica prison? I believe Mr. Borovic showed her a portion of the statement some days ago. This is 3D000001. That's the B/C/S. And 3 D 00-0126 for the English. Both versions have been scanned and are in the E-Court system. In order to expedite proceedings, I prepared a hard copy for Mrs. Bosanac. So if Mr. Usher could please assist me with this. We would like to have there displayed on the screen but maybe she will find it handier to actually use a hard copy. This is both the English version and the B/C/S. Can we please have the following page displayed in E-Court, 3D00/0110. That's for the B/C/S. For the English, 3D000181. [In English] English version. [Interpretation] Mrs. Bosanac, the green marker there should help you to find the right page. This is something that I prepared for you. If you could please turn up that particular page, the first that is marked in green. It says 345 at the top corner, the last three numbers, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please slowly read passage two. It starts with the words "Colonel Branko."

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Colonel Branko who conducted an interview with me and analysed what had happened, I wish to thank him sincerely, I believe it reads, for his humane treatment and giving me hope that there were peace loving or peace seeking people in the JNA, and people who want a peaceful coexistence of all the peoples in it these areas. He treated me in a fair manner both as a human being and as a doctor. Statement given by Vesna Bosanac, the 17th -- the 7th of November 1991. Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clarify, please. Colonel Branko was the man who interrogated you at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can see here that this statement is quite voluminous. Can you tell me how long the interrogation or interview lasted?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Mitrovica on the 21st of November, the date here is wrong. Obviously wrong. It says the 7th of November. It wasn't then. It was when I was leaving Mitrovica and perhaps in haste I wrote the date inaccurately. But the interview lasted until the 11th of November which means about three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be shown page 3D000136? That's the English version. B/C/S version is 3D000021.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would it be possible for my learned friend to call out the page number at the bottom of the English translation? I find that sometimes easier to find. If it's possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: English version is page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take the previous portion, Mrs. Bosanac. Take a look at what is marked in red and please refer to that page. The last three digits are 256; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please read out slowly the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean "in previous days"? "In previous days Dr. Njavro toured the ill and selected the wounded for convoy in accordance with his criteria among whom there were the most numerous were guards and civilians and, among them, was also a soldier of JNA Zivkovic, Ivan, who surrendered after being wounded."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when my colleague and I asked you about Ivan Zivkovic, you told us that you'd never heard that name?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you have to bear in mind that I wrote this statement after the fall of Vukovar and that in the following 14 years, I never gave a thought to this man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that case, if you have any doubts, it's better for you to say you don't know than to state something firmly.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you asked me whether I knew Ivan Zivkovic and the name didn't sound familiar. I wrote this 14 years ago, and I have no recollection of this name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you have recollection now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just read this, and of course I know that I wrote this down at the time, but in the meantime I forgot the name. Even now, I cannot assign a face to this name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell Their Honours who Ivica Arbanas was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivica Arbanas at the time, during the war, had a position -- I'm not sure what his position was, but he frequently came to the hospital to visit some wounded people. This is how his name is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do something in the police force?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a policeman, not in the sense of a policeman wearing a police uniform. He had a camouflage uniform similar to the one worn by the members of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the time, you knew that Arbanas wanted to keep Ivan Zivkovic there as a source of information?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I thought at the time but I couldn't be sure whether I saw this myself or this is something that he had told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to refresh your memory and tell you this: Do you remember that this soldier, Ivan Zivkovic, was supposed to be taken to Zagreb against his will? I assume that they wanted to interrogate him there. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really was not involved in compiling that list. Some civilians came to inquire whether they could join the convoy and were told no, that only the wounded could go with the convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please turn the next page? It's the same page for the English version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we might pause at this moment before you go to the next page. We will have a break now until just after a quarter to 4.00 and resume then. --- Break taken at 3.27 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us continue examining this document. I think that we are now on the page with the last three digits, 257?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for my learned from the Prosecution, we are still focusing on page 11 of the English translation. This first passage is quite a lengthy one and there is a sentence in it starting with the following words, "one of the members of the European mission ..." Would you please read that out.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "One of the members of the European mission noticed that in the hospital, and in front of the hospital," I suppose that's what it says, "there are a lot of Croatian soldiers." And then I replied that "in addition to security personnel, there was no one else except for those who were curious, the wounded, the family, those who were leaving."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to avoid any confusion, this pertains to the part of the statement dealing with the October evacuation. That part of your statement. At least that's how it looks to me. It pertains to the 18th of October 1991. Do you remember the dialogue you had with the representative of the European Monitoring Mission? That's how you called that person, although it must have been a person from Medecins Sans Frontieres. Would you please take a look at that page again.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that anyone from those NGOs or representatives of international organisations escorting the convoy, did any of them notice that there were a lot of soldiers in the hospital or around the hospital? Do you remember that detail?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that detail now. When I wrote this down it was probably something that was discussed. I remember that Mladen Jasreb [phoen] told me that once European monitors arrive, I should try and bring them to the municipal building to see Marin Vidic. I asked them when they arrived and they said that they couldn't go anywhere else because they were there in order to deal with evacuation, and then Marin Vidic and another person came to the hospital to talk to them. I did not participate in that conversation. I don't know what they talked about. But I know that in addition to the security personnel, there were no other soldiers in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that could not have been described as a lot of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I really don't know what that conversation pertained to. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let us conclude with these interrogations you were subjected to in Sremska Mitrovica, and what I put to you about the attitude that you had towards Colonel Branko. Was this statement taken under coercion? Did you put in that statement anything that wasn't true, that was inaccurate? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That entire situation in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica put me under huge pressure. The way I arrived there, the way I was admitted in there, the way I spent the first night in jail, those were very difficult, very bad conditions and, for me, it was a huge psychological shock, and an enormous pressure that I was put under. Once I arrived in the room with other women, when I was not alone any more, I went to those interrogations every day. In those interviews Colonel Branko treated me decently. The statement was not phrased precisely as I wanted to phrase it. I wanted to describe accurately the situation in Vukovar. However, he demanded that I write that in accordance with the instructions and questions he put to me. He told me not to write about the number of shells, the shooting, which I wanted to describe. He told me to leave that for later. Therefore, this statement was guided, guided by Colonel Branko, and I have to say that I experienced all kinds of things in that prison. I assume that you're not interested in that. When I was supposed to leave, or rather when I was transferred to Zagreb -- to Belgrade, the warden of the prison came suddenly --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not part of my question.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second. You asked me under what conditions I gave that statement and whether the statement was true. So I have to answer. So Colonel Branko asked me whether I could write in one sentence how he treated me. I wrote that down at that point in time, describing my feelings, and I was delighted because I was leaving the place. As for the other facts, I can't say specifically because I tried to write down things as I remembered them. The only thing that I wrote down inaccurately - and I remember it to this day - had to do with the circumstances surrounding my older son Damir. I stated there that he had left Vukovar earlier because he had been wounded and he was indeed wounded but he didn't leave earlier. In fact he didn't leave until the 17th in the evening. And as far as I remember, that was the only untrue item I put in in there. At the time I didn't know where my husband was, what had happened to him, what kind of complications he would face because of all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore? Are you rising?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No objection to that course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought I saw you trying to get to your feet. That will be received in evidence, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 45, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have many more questions left. And before I turn to another topic, I would like you to answer some questions concerning which my client gave me instructions in the course of the break. I asked you about the shelter of the hospital Crisis Staff and you gave me your answer. I have another question related to that. In the vicinity of the hospital, was there a shelter of the Crisis Staff of the Vukovar defence and Mr. Mile Dedakovic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated that that shelter was located in the yard of the building housing the Secretariat for National Defence, which is about 1 kilometre from the hospital, exactly across from the museum of Count Jelovac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are claiming that there was no shelter of the Crisis Staff of Mr. Mile Dedakovic in the makeshift housing 50 metres from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't. And in addition to that, there were no -- there was no makeshift housing there either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when were surgeon Jovic and the other two soldiers taken out of the hospital? When did they leave hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. All I know is that that afternoon, I saw in the 19th of November from my office, I saw Sasa talking to some soldiers near the door. Then I called out to him, towed him to go back to his room and to await the ICRC evacuation there. He said he would wait. But later I didn't see him. So I don't know when he left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember by any chance whether Mr. Sljivancanin asked you to see surgeon Jovic and the soldiers. Did he ask you whether he talked to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he not ask for that or do you not remember?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him asking that. And had he asked for that I would have sent somebody to fetch him just as I asked somebody to go fetch the doctor that he asked for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I'm interested in. When did he ask you to get in touch with Mrs. Gordana Mandic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening after the conversation with the ICRC. That could have been at around 8.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Evening?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before I was taken to Negoslavci, or perhaps at around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just correct the name in the transcript. The lady's name is Gordana Antic, right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who Ante Aric is, what did he do, how he ended up in your office and how did he come to be taken out of the barracks together with you and Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not taken out of the barracks. Ante Aric was a male nurse, and he came there to assist us, together with the doctors who arrived in late September of 1991. He was a male nurse. I don't know when he was taken out of the hospital and where to, or, rather, later in a conversation with him I heard that he had been taken to Negoslavci and that he even saw some wounded in the basement of a private house. I saw him when I was taken out of the barracks, when I was put in a Black Maria when I entered that vehicle, Dr. Njavro and Ante Aric were already there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Negoslavci after that conversation with Sljivancanin, when you were taken to this school where the temporary house -- temporary hospital was housed, were you bound?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody mistreat you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you were taken there in the presence of JNA colonel who was the head of that hospital? Does the last name Jovanovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. None of those people introduced themselves or mentioned their names. The only person who did introduce himself was Colonel Mrksic when I first arrived in Negoslavci. None of the other people I had contacts with introduced themselves. As for Veselin Sljivancanin, I realised it was him only when I was in prison when I saw in a magazine his photograph and a statement by him stating that he had liberated Vukovar. This is when I recognised him as Veselin Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to wrap this up I'll ask you a couple of questions. When you testified in chief, you said, when talking about the day of the evacuation, you had been waiting for the European monitors to arrive. You were under the impression that they were in a position to conduct the evacuation in an effective way; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't see them at that point; you only saw them later on in the prison at Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've been saying all these days that about 400 to 450 wounded were supposed to be evacuated, some seriously, some slightly wounded; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that on that day, 82 seriously wounded persons and 263 slightly wounded persons were evacuated, would you say that I'm wrong? Just say yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be wrong in saying that there remained another 52 wounded who were evacuated on the following day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact number is 54.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So I'm wrong. Would I be wrong in saying that 110 wounded decided to go back to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This information was provided by the European Monitoring Mission who actually attended the evacuation on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is people had been taken to Ovcara before the monitors arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please allow me to ask the question, if you will. Do you actually believe that this information is accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was an observation that ought to be heard. You have said what you want to say about the figure, have you, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I was just concerned you may have stopped the witness before she finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My final question is:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the witness place any trust in the European Monitoring Mission whom she had awaited so in those days?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, but I must say this again: They did not arrive at the Vukovar Hospital in time and for this reason, their information is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. This concludes my cross investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Doctor, I have been informed that you now no longer need to see the transcript of last Friday any further; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. I have the transcript in my possession. I have found out in the meantime that they were taken off the Internet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. So there is nothing you want to clarify about your evidence on Friday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. In that event, Mr. Moore, we can turn to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Re-examined by Mr. Moore:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I have a few very questions for you but may I deal with the first question? You were asked about the statement that was compiled and whether in actual fact you had signed it. Would you be kind enough, please, to look at the following document and confirm whether it is your signature on each and every page? I wonder if perhaps that could be done, please. The Court may remember that we went through the various details because the signature was missing because it was an abstract from the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's page 1. Can we just continue the process, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. This is Mira Medic's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough just to be shown the original document, please? It's sitting to your right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sure the doctor can be handed the document. It doesn't have to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are all those the pages that you've identified, doctor?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'd like you, please, or perhaps the Court Usher would be kind enough to turn to what I will call the English version, which you have there because it is in English, and go to the page 4 of 13, because you were asked questions about that. The bottom right-hand corner, 4 of 13?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can it be clarified for the claim what document it is that we are dealing with, please, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: This was the document that was cross-examined upon, whether in actual fact it was an English original, the process that was undertaken, because there was a discrepancy on what I will call page 4 of 13, whether in actual fact it was by November of 1991 or on November of 1991, if my memory serves me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that document marked identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was certainly cross-examined on and that topic was cross-examined on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: -- because there was a discrepancy between the Croatian and the Serbian translation, if I can put it in simplistic terms for me. It may well be that it was marked for identification but I'm absolutely certain that it was cross-examined on, on that topic. And there was questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No question of that. We are just trying to identify the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If it was marked, are you able to indicate the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: From my recollection, it wasn't marked as an exhibit per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was marked or it wasn't marked but the issue was -- well, twofold, one, was it signed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We understand that. Just we want to know whether it is a document that is in the system marked for identification or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So this is a fresh document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. It was the document cross-examined upon. Thank you very much. Could we turn, please, then to the area or the page where Dr. Bosanac was cross-examined on? That was 4 of 13. Are we able using our splendid technology to highlight the second paragraph of that, please, of the original document, which is in English? And, in English, is it right that the actual paragraph starts, "By November 1991"? The point was more for clarification. I think it was left really pending to assist the Court. There was a request for the original which we have now obtained. I'm entirely in the Court's hand in relation to that. I see no reason it should be made an exhibit but if issue is going to be taken on later proceedings then I would ask it be made an exhibit for clarification. I'm entirely in my learned friends' hands in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you identify the document by its date, and its nature for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It is the statement of Dr. Vesna Bosanac. It is dated, date of interviews are the 19th and 20th of June 1995 and the 21st and 23rd of July 1995. My hand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To whom was the statement made?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The statement was compiled with the assistance of two interpreters, one is a lady called Ivanka Anicic who apparently translated questions in English to Croatian and Croatian answers into English. That is on the 19th and 20th of June 1995. And then Mira Medic reading the English translation into Croatian to the witness on the 21st and 23rd of June. And the interpreter's certification, if my numbering is correct, would be 00327823.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I'm trying to get on to the record to whom the statement was made. Is it an interviewer by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is a statement compiled for the OTP and, as I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it was the subject of cross-examination, I think, by Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was. And he specifically dealt with "by November" or "on November." As I say, page 413. I wouldn't seek to make it an exhibit unless there was some issue in relation to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest that the document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document number will be 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I wonder perhaps if we -- if that is the case, for my part, OTP would like to retain the original unless there is any objection to that course, and a photocopy with the signatures being used for the Court. If, however, the Court wants the original, of course the Court must have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would suggest that once you've allowed the members of the Defence teams to sack the original, that unless there is any particular objection, that a photocopy version might become the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps while that's being done, I can continue in re-examination, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, you were asked about your participation as a doctor in the Vukovar Hospital. Throughout the period, and I will say September, October, and November, did you perform any operations on any patient?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps for completeness, if we go back, August and July, did you at any time perform operations on any patient in those months?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May we deal, then, please, with what I will call JNA soldiers being in a separate room? You're aware of the questions from the Defence on that topic. Why was it JNA soldiers were kept in a separate room in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because at the time when they arrived in the hospital, as wounded persons, the hospital was already overflowing with both wounded and civilians. Dr. Njavro and I believed it was a good thing to keep them apart so that Dr. Njavro could go and visit them. They were easily accessible. We believed that in this way they would not be facing any additional problems, such as being taunted by other patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. May we move on to the level of treatment of patients? There has been a suggestion that patients' treatment or perhaps lack of treatment was determined by ethnicity, namely that these soldiers and others of that same ethnic background or persuasion received lesser treatment. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. I felt taunted myself when I was asked those questions because that is just not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the principles that guided you as a doctor in the Vukovar Hospital over September, October, November, when we deal about treatment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I complied with all the professional guidelines and professional code of ethics. Those were the only guidelines that I followed, namely to help everyone who was sick or wounded and do the best job possible under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like you to be shown what I believe to be a Defence Exhibit, and I believe it to be Exhibit 43. It is a ruling apparently at the military court in Belgrade. Would you be kind enough to be shown that document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is not an exhibit, Mr. Moore. It's marked for identification as 43, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, doctor, have you got what I will call the little blue folder?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or, rather, I don't, I'm sorry, a blue folder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm hoping you've got the same colour as I have. Would you be kind enough to go to the very last divider which is a lime green?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at the first document after that, on the top right-hand corner, there seems to be page 270, 271, and then 272.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can't tell exactly what page we are referring to in that translation but you are asked and have been asked about an incident in the first half of November 1991, the wounded soldier Boban Gacic. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
