utterances.text: I need to find it first. Yes. I've got it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's at the top of page 271. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, you see what's particularised there, that he was brought to the hospital where he was operated upon. I won't go into the details. Do you have any recollection of such a person being brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember exactly what his injuries were?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember specifically. But I heard from my colleagues that he had been wounded and that as they were dressing his wounds, they noticed that this was an incipient case of gaseous gangrene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the first half of November. I'm not going to go into your faxes that you were sent or that you sent. Were you able or did you have the medication at that time to deal with gangrene gas?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had crystal penicillin at the time which we administered in booster doses more often than not. I state with full responsibility that all the medicines that we had in our possession were duly administered and all the steps were taken to save that soldier's life. I even remember my colleagues talking about what a wonderful lad he was. They even became friends and they felt sorry that he ended up involved in this war. I know that when he eventually died, everybody was greatly saddened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The second soldier that's referred to is the 13th of November, the following paragraph. That is a soldier called Ivica Nestorovic. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, here again it's alleged that you were informed about this young man but that you apparently denied him access to the hospital. Can you remember the circumstances in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is certainly not true. At this point in time, I no longer had any phone communication or any other form of communication with Borovo Komerc. I only heard later, once I'd been released from prison and reached Zagreb, about this patient, that he had been brought in, that he was seriously wounded, and that they weren't able to operate. But that they provided whatever assistance they could, whatever they had, despite which he died. I remember this because Colonel Branko kept asking me about these soldiers and he kept referring to Ivica Nestorovic who at the time I was not able to recall. It was later when I got to Zagreb that I heard about this person having been brought to Komerc. There was a makeshift hospital there as we know and some nurses were there. But I can't say that I recollect him being brought into the hospital, nor was I ever informed of his presence. Likewise, I need to add the following, now that we are talking about this subject matter. When cross-examining, counsel asked me if I knew who Dr. Kovacic was. I confirmed that I did but later I went back to this document and realised that the reference is probably not to the Dr. Kovacic I know but most likely to a different person. There is a reference here to Dr. Kuzmanovic's statement about the fact that Dr. Bosanac and Dr. Kovacic had been informed about this statement. The Dr. Kovacic I know was neither at Komerc nor at the hospital. Therefore, I don't think the reference is to the same doctor. And I can say nothing further about it. All I can say with certainty is that I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally I have one last question. You were asked by my learned friend Mr. Lukic about various lists and numbers, and you replied that you had a list of 97 people who were registered as wounded and subsequently killed in Ovcara. Do you still have that list or do you have that list with you now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have it in court with you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we refer to it, how was the list compiled?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received from the ministry, from the organisation of the defenders and mutual solidarity, and I had requested from the missing persons administration it in relation to Colonel Ivan Grujic that on the 20th of December 2005, which is when you visited Vukovar, to provide an accurate list, a last one, of persons identified from the mass grave at Ovcara. I realised that you had a list entitled missing persons. And I know that as time goes by, every Monday, more and more bodies are identified because this is an ongoing process. I requested this and asked them to send me a document which I intend to leave in the possession of the Tribunal. There is an attachment specifying the names of 192 persons whose bodies have been identified as executed at Ovcara. At this point I went back to our database, the one that we have discussed. I tracked down names of these same persons and we have managed to come up with a list containing the first and last names of 97 persons. This is the list that we discussed, and I have brought it along with me for my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough, please, to pass it to the usher? And perhaps if I could just look at it for a moment, please, with the Court's leave. If Your Honours would give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly it's a document I think that my learned friends have not seen. And I, for my part, feel that it would be an appropriate document for them to see at this stage. We would be seeking to make it an exhibit, at the moment, because it's just recently arrived. It is not in English, there is no translation for it, and it also involves graphs, bar charts, and other material. I, for my part, perhaps would submit that Defence should see it and if there is going to be any argument about it or a course to be adopted, it should be dealt with now. As matters stand, I would submit it is a document that should be made an exhibit, as it goes to a relevant issue in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would think that it -- before we go off the screen, 49 line 28, the date is given as 20 December 2005. That must be erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm told that it's the 20th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: 2005. And if there's an error then the error is not mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not concerned as to whose error but to get that right. Now, I would suggest that the document might again be made a document marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You would rely for its admission on the evidence which you have adduced from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it should now be made available in due course to the Defence and translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And at that point then you can return to the document to tender it as an exhibit, if there are no objections. If there are objections, to have those objections considered and ruled upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Exactly. And Your Honour may remember, and Your Honours may remember that I did indicate at the very outset that there was a documentation which the Defence -- the Prosecution only received last week, or I think it was the previous week, which was being translated. There was a difficulty in relation to the revealing of individuals' names who were still alive and are still alive but nominated as being military-involved on what I will call the Croatian side. And to some extent it overlaps I suspect with this document. So it may have its additional documentation to go with it. But perhaps if I could pass it now to the Defence, with the Court's leave and, as I say, and Your Honour has ruled that perhaps it can be marked for identification and be dealt with later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it could go to the Defence -- ah, are you saying -- I'm not quite sure why it should be right now that we delay while it goes to the Defence. That's my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, there is no need to delay as such. This would be my last topic of re-examination, and it may well be I only do it by way of caution, if there is any matter that should be raised, it should be raised perhaps before Dr. Bosanac would leave the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, do make it available now. I'm not sure that it gives the Defence any fair opportunity to examine the document in a few moments. That's why I felt it should now be marked and we simply wait until they have had full time to look at it and you have had a chance to have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then we could deal with the question of its admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder if any Defence counsel disagrees with that? I see nobody disagreeing. Oh, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one matter that I would like to raise and I think this is something that concerns all three Defence teams. That has to do with Mr. Moore's tactical approach when it comes to the presentation of this document. If before the examination-in-chief he told us that there was a document that he would later on send to us, and if we concluded our cross-examination in which we raised this issue, then we do not mind this document being marked as for identification. But we do have -- we want to be enabled to cross-examine this witness on the basis of this document, but we need to familiarise ourselves with the document first. And then once we do that, we would then tell the Chamber whether we want Mrs. Bosanac to come back to be examined on that issue alone. We simply cannot comprehend that a document is being introduced now at the end of cross-examination and not two weeks prior to this, only now after the cross-examination is concluded. This is why we would like this document to be given to us so that we can get acquainted with it and then after that, we can tell you whether we want to examine Mrs. Bosanac or perhaps Mr. Grujic on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Yes, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will be very brief. I have an objection to make. The Prosecution is in possession of this document several days now, and we think that they are not following the instruction of 48 hours. I think that they need to abide by the instructions set by the Trial Chamber. I fully agree with Mr. Lukic. An additional thing I want to raise is that we do not have the translation of this document and we are now denied an opportunity to cross-examine on this very important document. Therefore, we think that it can only be marked for identification; however, not admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Vasic? Could I mention before you speak that unless I have misunderstood things, there are two documents, not one. One was mentioned by Mr. Moore before he commenced the evidence of the witness. That was a document which he said had come into his possession, it was being dealt with, and as soon as it could be translated and made available, it would be. This second document is the one which Dr. Bosanac was now produced in court and made available to Mr. Moore. That is being moved, and that was called for in re-examination, because its existence became known to Mr. Moore during cross-examination by Mr. Lukic. It was Mr. Lukic that produced from the witness the information that she had this document containing this -- some 97 names. So this is a second document which no one of you, as Defence counsel, nor Mr. Moore as prosecuting counsel, knew about when adducing the evidence. Am I right in that, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. So be aware of that. With respect to the first document, Mr. Moore did indicate that when it was translated and could be made available, if there was a need for cross-examination, then, of course, that would need to be dealt with. With this new document, he at the moment wants it to go into evidence, the Chamber has indicated it should only be marked for identification to enable Defence counsel to have a look at it and, if there are difficulties with it, of course, then submissions will be put. I don't know whether that helps you, Mr. Vasic but I thought I would mention that before you made your further submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours. The situation you just described now is absolutely clear. I would like to support what my learned friends said. I also need to point out that my learned friend from the Prosecution, in the beginning of the examination-in-chief, stated that he had documents pertaining to the database in relation to the report sent by the Vukovar medical centre concerning the wounded and sick. It seems to me that this document that my learned friend just received from Mrs. Vesna Bosanac corresponds to that same database and represents a part of the documentation mentioned by my learned friend from the Prosecution. At any rate, perhaps the Prosecutor could tell us when he saw this document, was it during the proofing session or was it perhaps only today. But if I remember well, before the examination-in-chief, the Prosecutor told us that the examination-in-chief related to the newly discovered documents would be postponed until later date when the translations were ready and everything else could be prepared. It seems to me that the document we saw today in the courtroom comes from the same batch of documents and pertains to the same topics that my learned friend wanted to examine about at a later date in this trial. Therefore, I think that the comments of Mr. Lukic pertaining to the tactical approach of the Prosecution are very valid, as are his arguments about the need to enable the Defence to cross-examine on these documents, because this is something that is needed in order to ensure a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for the compliments about my tactical approach. Can I just deal with this issue. This document has come as a direct consequence of Mr. Lukic's cross-examination. I was not aware of this document. I noticed Mr. Lukic, having been told that the list existed, did not ask to see it. Therefore I asked for it to be shown in re-examination. I have indicated at the very outset of the trial that Dr. Bosanac had brought documentation which was documents that needed to be translated for everyone and there had been agreement between Prosecution and Defence that that should be deferred until the translation had been concluded and at an appropriate time for all parties. I do not know what this document says. Some of it is in B/C/S. Some of it relates to names, and I suspect diagnosis, and I suspect it is a compilation but I'm guessing. I suspect it is a compilation of documents that have been received or information received by Dr. Bosanac, and the database that existed at the hospital. But I can take it no further than that. All I'm submitting is, in re-examination I'm entitled to ask questions if a topic has arisen in cross-examination. The topic that arose here was that Dr. Bosanac said that she had a list to say that there was 97 people who were registered as wounded and killed at Ovcara. In my submission, that is a relevant issue. I have not tried to circumvent any rules. I have not tried to circumvent any rulings. I am quite happy to accommodate my learned friends as much as I possibly can. But there are two distinct criteria here: One, am I entitled to re-examine on the topic; the answer, I would submit, is yes. Two, if it's marked for identification, I have no problems in relation to that. But to make suggestions that I have behaved improperly is not correct. And I'm disappointed my learned friends should make such suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the Chamber's appreciation is that it was not clear to Defence counsel that there were two documents or that this was one that you had not previously seen and were unaware of. And I think that explains entirely their concerns and their submissions. And I am sure that, the position having been made clear, that that has cleared the air so to speak. The Chamber has grasped what you say. The Chamber, though, has taken the view that it should not yet be exhibited but merely marked for identification precisely to enable the Defence to have proper time to consider the document and the question then of its admissibility or not can be considered in due course. Not today. We are well conscious that it may unfortunately be necessary for the doctor to return to give evidence about the first list which you mentioned, which you say she brought with her --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- and, regrettable as that is, nevertheless it may be necessary for us to impose on the doctor to come again. That being so, there may arise an opportunity, if you pursue the tendering of this document, or should the Defence wish, to look at the question of whether cross-examination and examination on this further document should be allowed as a departure from the ordinary procedure. And we will certainly consider that if either Prosecution or the Defence wish to proceed along that route when there has been time to look at this further document and assess it in light of what else is known. So all of that will remain for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, the document -- does it bear a date or a heading that we can readily identify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It has a date which seems to be the 20th of October. There seems to be a reference of 519/08/05/2. And the recipient is Dr. Vesna Bosanac, and the signature is a ministry signature from Zagreb, and it seems to be Grujic, Grujic. And for completeness it appears to be a list of 192 names with dates of birth, and I suspect locations of birth. Then another chart that seems to be compiled with 97 names, dates of birth, names and, I suspect, diagnoses. And then added to it are a number of what I will call bar charts in B/C/S, and the document will remain as one. It is clear that someone has done an analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The document you describe will be received, marked only for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be number 47.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you will provide copies of that to the Defence and translations of it as soon as is practicable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you will provide the original now, please, to the Registry so that there can be a copy of it now put into the record. You will then get it back for the purpose of copying, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have a question, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I would like to clarify something concerning this document. I received from the ministry the letter that was just admitted here, and an enclosure containing a list of 192 identified persons killed in Ovcara. This chart and a graph that were enclosed came from the analysis that we conducted at the hospital where we compared the list of those killed and identified in Ovcara and the database that Mr. Moore spoke of earlier. I thought that this clarification would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. I think we can leave it at that, and it will be a question for later whether further questioning about this document is necessary and appropriate. Are there any further questions, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There are no further questions, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, for the moment, I'm glad to be able to tell you that concludes the course of evidence. As you have understood, it may become necessary for you to be called back to deal with these further issues. When -- whether that will occur and when it may be, I can't tell you at the moment. May we, though, thank you for coming. We appreciate you had the difficulty of travelling with an injury, and we thank you for your assistance. We will, I think, rise now. It will be a convenient time for a break. And that will enable the doctor, then, to leave the Court. I did mention on Friday that as this was the first day of late sittings, we would adjourn earlier as a gentle break-in for everybody to the new times, but tomorrow, prepare to sit through until 7.00. Today, at a time convenient, around 6.15, we will adjourn for the day. We will resume now at 5.15. --- Break taken at 4.56 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it Mrs. Tuma that will be taking this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could have the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please take the card that is given to you and read the affirmation aloud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mrs. Tuma will ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Tuma:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar my apologies for making you wait a couple of hours before starting this afternoon's session and are you comfortable?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Kolesar, what kind of profession do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you for this. I'm learning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar could you please tell us in the courtroom what kind of profession you have?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I'm a retired nurse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I retired in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you please tell us about your educational background? When you were trained in your profession?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Following secondary school, I went to a three-year medical school for nurses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was -- when did you examine as a nurse?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was it?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I completed the medical school for nurses in Osijek, and I have worked in the hospital in Vukovar since 1961.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what capacity? You were working as a nurse but was there a specific capacity you were working in the Vukovar -- the hospital Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I worked as a registered, meaning senior, nurse. From 1962 to 1991 I was head nurse in the surgical ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your superior in your -- in the surgery ward? Now we are talking about 1991 from the fall, spring, summer, and fall 1991.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: From 1988 and on, Dr. Mladen Ivankovic was head of the surgical ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the director of the hospital in -- during the spring of 1991 and was it changed later on, and what time, and how was the change done?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: In 1991, Dr. Rade Popovic was director of the hospital. In the course of the summer, either in June or in July, a change occurred. Dr. Popovic was no longer the director, but, rather, Dr. Vesna Bosanac was appointed director.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the reason for the change of director of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: No, no. This had nothing to do with my work. It did not affect my work in any way, this change of director, and I couldn't tell you the real reason for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many nurses were you supervising, Mrs. Kolesar, when you were working as a chief nurse? Now we are talking about spring, summer, and autumn of 1991, just to make us to show your capacity as a chief nurse.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The job of the head nurse in the surgical ward was to control and educate medical staff or, rather, to monitor and educate the medical staff and janitors. There were about 100 nurses and about 25 janitors or cleaning ladies. In addition, there were also medical technicians who worked in the surgical ward as plaster technicians or they worked in the clinic itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. I will move on and ask you to describe just briefly about the setup of the hospital in peace time and, let us say, before May 1991. How many beds could the hospital take for the total number of patients at the time? Now we are talking about before May 1991.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The hospital had about 400 to 450 beds. Perhaps 420 would be the most accurate figure. It had almost all wards, paediatrics, neurology, psychiatry, surgery, gynaecology, so all wards were represented. We also had full diagnostical capabilities and the full capacity of the hospital was 450 patients. All wards operated normally. The hospital was very well equipped. One part of it was new, the other part was renovated, and the work was conducted absolutely normally. The hospital was part of the medical centre. The medical centre included health clinics which provided primary health care. So the total number of employed staff members in the entire medical centre was 900 to 950.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. When it comes to the ethnicity of patients and medical staff, were there any kind of differences or was it a mixture or was it any kind was prevailing the other sort of ethnicity amongst the patients and the medical staff at this time?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: It made absolutely no difference what the ethnic background of a patient was. There were no problems with the personnel. All of us worked together. One couldn't say that there were more people of this ethnic background than that ethnic background. Perhaps there were more Serb doctors, but as for the other staff members, they were all equally represented. One couldn't tell that one ethnic group dominated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your, as a chief nurse at the hospital, and supervising other nurses, the principle that guided your work as a nurse towards the patients? What kind -- what treatment did you give the patients? When there any differences when it comes to ethnicity in that sense?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: There is no such principle known to the science of medicine and the same applies to nurses. Doctors take an oath and the same treatment is accorded everyone and the same applies to nurses. All patients are always treated equally. The staff, too, are treated equally regardless of their position. This is the guiding principle in all hospitals, I should assume. As for the medical staff, I appreciated honest, hard-working people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it also regardless of what kind of conditions the staff, medical staff, was working under?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The same thing. There were no better or worse conditions, as it were. There were some jobs that were perhaps a bit easier and some that were a bit more difficult, but this in no way was affected by the ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank, Mrs. Kolesar. I suppose you're aware of an event that happened on the 2nd May 1991, when some Croat policemen were killed. Did that event create any kind of differences in the setup of the hospital or personnel and patients?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: It is certain that the 2nd May of 1992 very much affected everything that from then on happened in town, not to the same extent in the hospital, I would say, with the possible exception of our surgery ward. After the 2nd of May, they always had to be prepared to admit a certain number of wounded on any given day. Up to that point, we had no special beds that were awaiting wounded people. On the 2nd of May we had to start improvising and start discharging patients that were nearing full recovery, in order to make room for the wounded police officers and wounded civilians alike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have any special affect on the kind of patients --

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: This certainly affected both ethnic groups. Everybody who was on their way to the surgery ward was having second thoughts. Do I really have to go there? Is this really necessary? There was a lot of confusion about town and no one was certain what would happen, whether the JNA attacks would continue or not. At any rate, the entire hospital was fully operational and this includes all the wards, with the exception of the surgery ward. They had to have a certain number of beds available and a greater number of doctors and nurses available for emergencies and for any wounded people coming in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crisis committee, Mrs. Kolesar, can you please describe what that is? And when it -- what it was and when it was set up and for what reason.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was established as early as the month of May or perhaps early June. Its purpose was to prepare the hospital to admit a greater number of patients than was the norm. Of course, the hospital had more beds than were being used but the question was, were these adequate conditions? For example, if there was an attack against the hospital and work became impossible in the surgical theatres, they had to be moved elsewhere where they could continue to operate normally. The purpose of the Crisis Staff was to provide a make shift facility to provide sufficient staff and to provide supplies in terms of water, electricity, medicine, everything you need to treat a patient. The Crisis Staff comprised the chief of surgery, the director, the chief nurse, the chief nurse of the surgery ward, and all the chiefs of all the departments that were deemed to be helpful in this emergency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were at the time in May 1991, any kind of preparation so to say made in the hospital in order to facilitate if there should be any ongoing attacks on the silty itself and that could have any kind of impacts on the hospital as such?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: When the new wing of the hospital was built back in 1975 or 1976, one of the conditions imposed was that an atomic shelter should be built. Therefore the hospital had ha atomic shelter and this was a safe area. It was never used and it was never maintained. It was never meant to be used for medical work until Borovo Selo happened. It was at this point that during the summer, that means in June, July and August, the atomic shelter was redone in a manner of speaking so that it could be used by both doctors and patients but it only had four small rooms with some auxiliary rooms. There was a -- there was a surgical theatre and a room used by duty doctors. We set up equipment in the basement, and this was now the room where operations were performed and intensive care administered. This was a matter of necessity. In addition to that, there were sporadic attacks by the JNA on Vukovar throughout the summer and we at the Crisis Staff worked out a detailed plan of how the wounded would be evacuated from the wards into the atomic shelter. The two buildings were connected by an underground corridor. Midway down the corridor was the door to the atomic shelter. Therefore all the wards that were on the first and second floor had priority in being evacuated. The ground floor came last. Unfortunately, there was an attack that occurred about the 15th of August, an attack on Vukovar, and this was a test, as it were, on how the atomic shelter would be used in the future. All the patients were taken to the atomic shelter and, once the attack was over, they were returned to their respective wards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. I will now move on to show to the Court and also to the parties here a chart that has been disclosed to the Defence as well, and that is a description of the hospital so that we all know that we are talking about and what kind of -- so all can see when Mrs. Kolesar is made a reference to the atomic shelter or the corridor so we know what we are talking about here. And that is a chart with an ERN number 04639058, for the Court officer, and I guess it also has been disclosed to the Defence as well. Have everyone access and also the witness access on the screen to that document?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I can see it. I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, do you recognise this drawing?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: This is an expromptu drawing which represents the hospital buildings. You can see the road and you can see the Danube. You can even see the connecting corridor running between the new building and the so-called old building of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mrs. Kolesar. Who has made this drawing?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Some days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And I will just give information for the Defence and for the Court that this drawing was made by Mrs. Kolesar during the proofing the other day, last week. And it's not signed. I would like to add that. But it has been identified by Mrs. Kolesar as done by her. And I would like later on to admit this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar now we move on to give us, please, a description of the hospital. We have been earlier talking about the old building, the new building and the corridor and atomic shelter. Can you please show on this drawing the different kinds of parts of the hospital that you have been talking about? Can anyone show the witness how she will do that, please? Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: This is an amateur drawing, but I hope that we can use it to clarify the respective positions of everybody involved, where people worked and where people stayed. I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You were talking about the atomic shelter. Can you please show on this chart where the atomic shelter were located?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, there would be a paper copy and we could put it on the overhead perhaps, and see where the pointings are made?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, we have paper copies as well. Yes. Okay. Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The atomic shelter is actually between the two buildings, between the so-called old hospital and the so-called new hospital. It's linked to an underground corridor connecting the two buildings. It's between the new section and the old section of the hospital. There is an underground corridor that connects the two buildings. There is an entrance and it comprises four large rooms and several smaller rooms used for storage for keeping supplies, or even for cooking meals. There are two lavatories included.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the old building and the new building that you mentioned earlier, can you show on the chart where the new building and where the old billing is?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: This is the old building, and to the left is the new building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the corridor that is connecting the old and the new building, can you please show that, Mrs. Kolesar?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: It's right here. I'll underline it. The size here on this sketch does not correspond with its actual size on the spot, but it more or less represents the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can you please also Mrs. Kolesar show us the whole hospital area, if there were any gates into the hospital area from any kind of road.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The entire hospital area is made up of an area leading from the road to a parking lot in front of the hospital, and then you have the main entrance with the reception area. If you take this entrance, you're able to access all the wards and all the rooms of the hospital. Across the yard, you have a section which is also adjacent to a road. Here again there is an entrance to the hospital. There is a roundabout here which can easily be accessed by an ambulance and patients requiring urgent assistance can be transported to the hospital more expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. You just mentioned across the yard. Where is the yard in the hospital area? Can you please mark that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: It is actually between the two buildings, the old and the new, and it extends to an area which is behind the new building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the emergency exit? Where is that located on the chart, please?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The emergency exit was only here in the surgery ward. That was the only one. I am marking it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The surgery clinic, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: We can put the map or the chart aside and we can go back to the chart later on in the examination-in-chief. Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. This was for a description for the parties in order to have some idea of, and also for myself, how the setup of the hospital were at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, when started the real attack on Vukovar city? When was that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I think it coincided with the 2nd of May, although that was an event of local significance and only a handful of police officers were attacked. However, from that time on, the JNA vehicles were continually in motion leaving the barracks and going, for example, to Borovo Selo. So we would come across many of those although they had not yet started firing and pounding us, but their presence was permanent. And then in June or July, there were sporadic attacks. I'm no military expert myself, but it certainly seemed that the attacks were being launched either from a ship on the Danube or from across the Danube, from the opposite river bank, because that's what the impacts indicated, the way the houses that were hit were hit. For example, today I see a building it's intact. The next morning I go to work and I see that these same buildings have in the meantime been destroyed which started changing the cityscape. The first major attacks happened in Borovo Selo. There were several major attacks especially in July and August. And the wounded that were -- that started coming in at the time were coming in from Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mrs. Kolesar you're talking about the major attacks in June and July. Was it other attacks than the city itself? Were there other areas that were targeted as well, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Of course. The neighbouring villages must have been targeted too, I assume, because at a later date I saw that they had been destroyed. I'm not sure about the timing but if we are talking about the town and its surroundings, I'm mentioning Borovo Naselje, I can also mention Luzac. Throughout the summer, I can't say there were daily attacks but there certainly were attacks occurring every now and then. What were the reasons behind these attacks and what had prompted them is not something that I can judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, you just mentioned some villages in the neighbourhood of Vukovar city. How far away from Vukovar city were those villages located?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The largest settlement in the surroundings of Vukovar is the town of Ilok and the distance between Vukovar and Ilok is 35 kilometres. It was part of Vukovar municipality, and needless to say, the people of Ilok went to Vukovar to receive medical treatment. They only had a local health centre there. All the other villages Opatovac, Stompajvci [phoen], Tolonik [phoen], and so on and so forth were a little closer, distances being 9 kilometres, 20 kilometres and so on and so forth. On the opposite side you had Borovo Selo, the distance being perhaps nine or ten kilometres or not even that much. Trpinja was very close. Brsadin was 8 or 9 kilometres, Petrovci, 9, Negoslavci likewise. They all went to the Vukovar Hospital to receive medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All those -- do I understand you right, Mrs. Kolesar, when you -- do you mean that all those villages or cities you were mentioning right now, they were -- that they were all shelled throughout June and July 1991 and that the hospital received wounded patients from those areas?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. The wounded from Novi Cakovci there had been an attack at some point in the summer. They came in, they were wounded, and they were all civilians. About five or six persons were admitted. They managed to reach the Vukovar Hospital at this early stage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time frame, June and July 1991, was the hospital itself attacked at any point in the summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Yes. I was just about to say that. The section with the surgical theatres had been targeted from the Danube, from the river. The buildings were in danger. They had not caved in yet but several shells landed on the hospital roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, June, July we are talking about, was there any marking of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: We are talking about the month of July. The hospital was marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what way, then, and where, please?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: It was marked. There was a huge red cross out in the yard. Given the fact, though, that the new building was very tall, it wasn't possible to place the cross on top of the building. So the Red Cross was placed on the roof of the infection ward, which was a little bit lower than the surrounding buildings. One thing is for sure, however. The hospital was visibly marked. One mark being out on the lawn between the two buildings and the other being on the roof of the infection ward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, you have on your right-hand the chart that you were so kind enough to draw the other day so we can see it more clearly. Can you please show on that chart where the marking of the hospital was at the time?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The marking was at the parking lot. It was a concrete area behind the new building. The other sign was on the roof of the infection ward building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say that those markings were clearly visible?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I assume they had been arranged in such a way as to be clearly visible. The people whose job it was to put those up seemed certain that they would be sufficient to clearly mark the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: We can leave the chart for a moment again. And then I would like to move on to the time period between August and up to mid-November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time frame, were you living in the city of Vukovar or were you at any point of time moving into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: I live in the town of Vukovar itself, close to the centre of town. I made these daily trips to the hospital from my home, from where I live. I went to work every day regardless of what I was seeing along the way on a daily basis, things being demolished, houses destroyed that used to be in perfect condition. We continued to go to work all the way until the 25th of August when this changed. On the 25th of August, the town itself was subjected to a heavy aviation attack. Lots of wounded started streaming into the hospital. All the wounded from all the other wards had been taken to the atomic shelter or to the hospital basement. Until the 20th of November not a single wounded person and not a single bed were ever returned to any of the wards. Between the 25th of August and the 20th of November, all the hospital tasks were performed in the basement, in the underground corridors and in the atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of the hospital was not able to be in use due to the attacks? And was that from a specific point in time?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Well, from that time on, from the 25th of August onwards, the staff working there and the patients were facing grave danger, and operations were no longer performed in the surgery ward. For a while, these continued in the gynaecology ward on the first floor but that too became dangerous after a while because all the window panes had been shattered and there was no way to keep the room sterile. From the very beginning of the aggression against Vukovar, but more specifically from late August onwards, those could no longer be used. We used the equipment from those rooms but we no longer used the rooms themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mrs. Kolesar, you just mentioned that on the 25th of August, there was an aviation attack. Can you tell us more about that and about how that affected the people, and if you could see any consequences in your -- in terms of your profession as a nurse at the hospital? Were there civilians or people coming into the hospital as wounded? Can you tell us more about that, please?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: The attack on the 25th was extremely fierce. A very large number of civilians were killed because they were not prepared for something like that. So I can say that this attack surprised both them and us. Later on, the people start living the so-called basement lives. Everybody hid in their own neighbourhoods where they could find shelter in their basements and so on. Therefore, later on, even though the attacks became even more fierce, fewer civilians were injured or killed because people became more careful. They stopped using their houses and they only used the basement areas and practically lived underground. The wounded could be brought to the hospital in our hospital vehicles. We still had water and electric supply, and, if our ambulances went to the spot, they would bring the wounded back to the hospital. Sometimes the wounded would be transported in private vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, on the 25th of August you just mentioned that there was a large number of civilians that was wounded and killed. Do you have today any kind of recollection how many, about, patients were coming to the hospital on that day?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Definitely 30 to 40, definitely 30 to 40 people were wounded. What I'm trying to say is that all of these people received treatment in our hospital. They were all admitted into hospital. The advantage at the time was that the roads leading to Vinkovci and their hospital were still open so one could travel through Bogdanovci, Marinci, Nustar, and reach Vinkovci. We treated the seriously wounded and operated on them and did everything we could but we also evacuated them so as not to subject them to the conditions that I described, meaning living in the atomic shelter and improvised areas. That in turn enable us to be ready for the influx of new patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mrs. Kolesar you just mentioned 30 to 40 patients that got to the hospital on the 25th of August 1991. Were they -- what kind of people were they, the 30 to 40 people that arrived to the hospital on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Normal, scared and wounded people. There were children among them, women, senior men and women. Just residents of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Normal civilians, people, then, was it so?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Civilians, yes. Most of them were civilians. I can't say whether there was among them perhaps a uniformed defender or somebody else. They were also sometimes wounded and for us they were just regular patients. Anybody who was wounded at any time, any member of any army, was admitted and treated just like any other patient. The treatment that civilians or any other uniformed persons received was absolutely identical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And earlier you mentioned here, Mrs. Kolesar, that you went -- you travelled between your home and the hospital. Was there any time that you couldn't do that and, if so, why?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Since my house is near the hospital, I normally went on foot. After the 25th of August, perhaps occasionally I could have gone home when there were fewer attacks and so on, but my presence at the hospital was necessary because it was questionable whether we would be able to return to the hospital if we went home. There was that possibility that, due to attacks, we would be unable to go back to work in the hospital, and this pertained not only to me but to all other staff members who lived in Vukovar and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, on your daily walks between your home and the hospital before you moved so to say to the hospital, what did you see around you in the morning and in the afternoon or in the evening when you were walking between, and what changes do you see during those days when you were looking around on your daily walk so to say between your house and the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: En route, every day, one could see new destruction. What I wish to say is that one could be injured while en route. More and more buildings were destroyed. The road was also damaged, hit. One day, the drivers tried to drive me home and it was almost impossible to drive on the road leading to my house because of all the potholes caused by shells, bombs and so on. Therefore, all of the roads were damaged and it was very difficult to drive to the hospital or anywhere else from one part of the town to the other one, because of the damaged roads. Likewise, it was very difficult to transport the wounded, because of these roads. As for the houses, there were daily new destructions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about -- how was the medical staff? Could they -- were they compelled, so to say, any point in time to move to the hospital or could they, as you, Mrs. Kolesar, walk between or travel between the home and the hospital? And how about their families?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Most of the nurses and even doctors, naturally, wanted to spend the night in their own homes, under normal circumstances. Their children, spouses, families, lived in basements. They went home because their shifts would be such that they worked for 24 hours and then were free for 24 hours. Therefore, they didn't need to spend that free time in the hospital. If it was possible, they went back home, but we also needed to be sure that they would be able to come back to the hospital when they needed -- when we needed them. And this was the system that was in place up until September, and every morning we would be awaiting the arrival of our staff. We also had to draw up new schedule, depending on who arrived to work that day. And this applied both to nurses and to the cooks, cleaning ladies and so on. We needed to make sure that all of the work could be performed. Therefore, this system was in place up until the end of September when it became almost impossible to anybody to go home, except for the people who lived right next to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was this so, Mrs. Kolesar?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: This was so because new destruction was continuously inflicted on the city. It was impossible for these people to spend time in their apartments or in their houses. There was no safety for them, or, rather, they felt safe only when they had their families with them. As a result of that, five, six, or ten nurses brought their children to the hospital, aged between 2 and, say, 15 years. So for me personally, it was easier to make a roster and to organise the work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time frame when we are talking about August and November, when it comes to patients that got to the hospital, that were wounded, how many patients at an average, every day, would you recall that received treatment or went to the hospital in order to be treated?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: On average, we had about 30 wounded persons. There were days when we had ten and there also were days when we had 80 of them. It all depended on the ferocity of the JNA attacks, either aviation attacks or shelling attacks. So there were different days when there were days when we could treat somebody efficiently and quickly, and there were such days when it was impossible to provide immediate assistance to all 80 of the wounded. We had to do triage. We had to give priority to those who were most seriously wounded. However, everybody received treatment in the conditions that prevailed at the time. Not a single person was left unattended. Everybody received a tetanus shot or an antibiotic or was operated on. After that, we placed them in the rooms that we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. When it comes to those average of 30 wounded a day about, what kinds of nationalities were there amongst those people and what kind of people were there? Were there civilians or were there armed soldiers? Can you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Most of them were civilians but, naturally, there were wounded defenders. That was unavoidable. There was no other hospital that they could have gone to. So this hospital was open both for civilians and wounded defenders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: Up until the 19th of October, we had organised convoys which enabled us to send away some of the wounded. So, while the road through the cornfields was still open, we were able to transport elsewhere the most seriously wounded persons. And the last occasion when such persons were evacuated was on the 19th of October when we evacuated 120 severely wounded persons. That in turn enabled us to admit new patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. We will come to that in a while. How was the conditions in the hospital? How was -- was there any changes in the conditions, working conditions, in the hospital, due to the attacks on the hospital itself? Could you perform surgery? Were there water? Were there electricity? Were there medicine and food for the patients?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: In September, in early September, and up until mid-September, we still had normal supply of electricity and water. Following that, we had neither electricity nor water. Electricity came from a generator, and water came from water supplies. Our water reserve contained 12.000 litres of water. We used that for our daily work and then we needed to refill it. So in order to have a steady supply of water, we had to constantly bring in or transport water. The main assistance in that regard was provided by the firemen who used their cisterns to transport water for us. The water was placed in water depots and we used approximately two and a half thousand litres of water a day in order to prepare food, wash laundry, to wash patients and to perform surgeries. Electricity was supplied by generators. We received some generators from the Borovo factory. We never had to suspend any surgeries due to lack of water or electricity. So we had to ensure that we had sufficient quantities of laundry water in order to have normal sanitary conditions, and enough electricity in order to conduct operations.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR
utterances.text: These were certainly not normal working conditions. I don't know if you can imagine daily life of so many people under such circumstances. When we had only the minimum needed to ensure sanitary conditions. We had to make sure that what we feed them was not poisonous, that it was not contagious. We had to make sure that lavatories operated in normal conditions. We had to make sure that our patients had beds that were clean enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I think we can end there for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tuma. As you realised we reached the time when we were to adjourn today. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15. Mrs. Kolesar, I must ask you if you would return tomorrow to continue your evidence at 2.15 in the afternoon. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
